analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers erase private student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill got a hearing and a favorable 6-3 subcommittee vote but never reached a House floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2005 bankruptcy law, private student loans — loans from banks and lenders, not the federal government — can only be wiped out if the borrower proves "undue hardship," a standard so strict that most people never qualify. This bill would strike that protection, letting private student loans be discharged in bankruptcy just like credit card debt and medical bills. The change applied only to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, so it would not have changed any existing case.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers drowning in private student loan debt. Today they can escape those loans only by proving "undue hardship" — essentially that they cannot maintain a minimal living and will never be able to pay — which courts rarely find. The bill would have let them treat private student loans like any other unsecured debt in bankruptcy, restoring the pre-2005 rule.

how_it_helps.text: Removes private student loans (and certain other educational payments) from the list of debts that bankruptcy cannot erase, amending section 523(a)(8) of the bankruptcy code.
Keeps the exception only for loans funded by government units or nonprofits, so purely private bank loans would be dischargeable like credit card or medical debt.
Applies only to bankruptcy cases filed on or after enactment, leaving existing discharges and cases untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders, whose collateral is currently protected: they lend knowing the debt generally cannot be wiped out in bankruptcy. If dischargeability returned, lenders would face more bankruptcy risk on this lending, which lenders said would mean fewer or more expensive private student loans.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and some economists argued that restoring dischargeability would raise interest rates or reduce the availability of private student loans, because lenders would price in the risk of bankruptcy discharge — an argument credited when Congress extended the exception to private loans in 2005.

The bill would not have helped federal loan borrowers, whose loans would remain non-dischargeable except in the government/nonprofit categories; only the private-loan segment of the student debt crisis would get relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to struggling borrowers is real and targeted: people facing genuine financial ruin would regain a last-resort exit that credit card borrowers have always had. The main cost is that private student loans could get somewhat more expensive or harder to get, a trade-off Congress consciously made in the other direction in 2005. The bill was drawn narrowly — prospective only, and leaving government-backed loans' treatment intact — which limits but does not eliminate the cost side.

outcome.mechanism: It got a hearing and a favorable 6-3 vote in a House Judiciary subcommittee, but the full committee never took it up and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2010 by Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) with Rep. Danny Davis (D-IL), and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee held a hearing on April 22, 2010.
On September 15, 2010, the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law forwarded the bill to the full committee by a 6-3 vote.
The full Judiciary Committee never marked up or reported the bill, and no chamber ever voted on it; the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders are better off, because the bankruptcy shield that makes their loans hard to escape survived the Congress. Student borrowers remain unable to discharge private student loans except under the near-impossible undue-hardship standard.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing and forwarded the bill to the full committee on a 6-3 vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Full committee under Chairman John Conyers Jr. (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after the subcommittee forwarded it; no markup or report before the Congress ended.

against.name: Private student loan lenders
against.what_they_did: Opposed restoring bankruptcy dischargeability for private student loans, having supported the 2005 law that extended the exception to them.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no House Republican sponsored the bill, and the full Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped the bankruptcy shield that lets these lenders collect even from borrowers in financial ruin. That shield was the industry's own lobbying achievement in the 2005 bankruptcy law, and its removal would have exposed lenders to discharge risk they currently do not bear.
